The Civil Rights Movement, Supplementary Reading

Women of the Movement

The organizers, educators, and activists whose work made the movement possible, and whose names rarely appear in textbooks.

The Civil Rights Movement is often taught as the story of a few famous speeches and charismatic male leaders. That version is incomplete. The movement ran on the daily labor of women, who organized boycotts, trained activists, registered voters, and sat at lunch counters while crowds screamed at them. This page introduces six of those women. As you read, think about why their stories were left out, and what that absence tells us about how history gets written.

The Boycott Era
1955
Jo Ann Robinson 1912–1992 Organizer

When Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, most people imagine that a protest movement slowly built over days or weeks. In reality, the Montgomery Bus Boycott was operational within 48 hours, because Jo Ann Robinson had been planning it for over a year.

Robinson was an English professor at Alabama State College and the president of the Women's Political Council, a Black professional women's organization that had already drafted a boycott plan and written letters to city officials demanding better treatment on Montgomery's buses. When Parks was arrested, Robinson stayed up through the night cutting and distributing 52,000 flyers calling for a one-day boycott.

The boycott worked on Day 1 before MLK had given a single speech. Robinson organized the logistics. King was asked to lead the movement she had already started. Robinson later wrote about this period in her memoir, but her name almost never appears in textbooks.

Worth Noting

Robinson took a serious personal risk. Alabama State College was a state institution, its president warned her that using college equipment for civil rights organizing could cost her the job. She did it anyway.

Top: Jo Ann Robinson, Alabama State College professor and Women's Political Council president. Bottom: Robinson's arrest mugshot from civil rights organizing activities.
Rosa Parks 1913–2005 Activist / NAACP
The Myth

Rosa Parks was a tired seamstress who spontaneously refused to give up her seat one day, sparking a movement by accident. She was not politically active before that moment.

Nearly everything about that version is false. Parks had been a committed civil rights activist for over a decade before her arrest. She was the secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee, a training center for civil rights and labor organizers, just months before her arrest.

Parks had also personally traveled to Scottsdale, Alabama to support the family of Recy Taylor, a Black woman who had been gang-raped by six white men in 1944. That investigation, which Parks led for the NAACP, went nowhere legally, but it shows who she was long before 1955.

Her refusal on the bus was deliberate. The Women's Political Council had already been looking for the right person to anchor a boycott challenge, someone whose background could withstand intense public scrutiny. Parks was chosen carefully because she was exactly the kind of person who could.

"People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in."

— Rosa Parks
Top: Rosa Parks portrait, 1955. Bottom: Parks being fingerprinted by Montgomery police after her arrest, December 1, 1955.
Building the Infrastructure
1957 – 1961
Septima P. Clark 1898–1987 Educator / Organizer

Martin Luther King Jr. called Septima Clark "the mother of the movement." That is not an exaggeration. Clark developed the organizing model that made mass voter registration possible across the South.

In the late 1950s, Clark created the Citizenship Schools on Johns Island, South Carolina, small community literacy programs designed to teach Black adults to read well enough to pass the rigged literacy tests that kept them off voter rolls. The schools were held in homes and beauty parlors to avoid white retaliation.

The model worked so well that SCLC adopted it nationally. Clark trained hundreds of local teachers who then ran their own Citizenship Schools across the South. By the early 1960s, the program had directly helped register tens of thousands of voters, the same voters who would march in Selma and demand the Voting Rights Act.

Clark was also fired from her teaching job by the state of South Carolina in 1956 for being an NAACP member. She lost her pension. She kept organizing.

"I was on the executive staff of SCLC, but the ministers didn't respect women too much."

— Septima Clark, on working within the movement's own hierarchies
Top: Clark (third from left) at the Highlander Folk School, Tennessee, the training center for civil rights organizers. Bottom: Clark in later years.
Ella Baker 1903–1986 Organizer / SNCC Founder

Ella Baker spent decades doing the unglamorous work that makes movements function: recruiting members, training organizers, building networks, and traveling to small towns where nobody was watching. She worked for the NAACP through the 1940s, became the first executive director of SCLC after the Montgomery Boycott, and then did something unexpected.

When college students launched the sit-in movement in 1960, Baker called a conference at Shaw University and helped them form their own independent organization, SNCC, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. She deliberately kept it separate from SCLC and from King's leadership.

Baker believed the movement needed to be led from the bottom up, not top down. She was skeptical of the "charismatic leader" model, worried that if the movement depended on one man's presence, it would collapse without him. SNCC's structure, young, local, decentralized, was her design.

That tension between Baker's grassroots model and King's SCLC is part of why the movement eventually fractured. Stokely Carmichael, who would coin the phrase "Black Power," came out of the SNCC tradition Baker built.

"Strong people don't need strong leaders."

— Ella Baker
Top: Baker speaking at a civil rights rally. Bottom: Baker portrait.
Direct Action
1960 – 1963
Diane Nash 1938–present SNCC / Freedom Rides

Diane Nash grew up in Chicago, attended Fisk University in Nashville, and was shocked by segregation when she arrived in the South. Within a year she had become one of the most effective direct-action strategists in the entire movement.

Nash co-founded SNCC and led the Nashville sit-in campaign in 1960, which was one of the most disciplined and successful in the country. When the Nashville mayor asked the protesters to stop, Nash looked him in the eye in front of a crowd and asked: "Mayor West, do you feel it is wrong to discriminate against a person solely on the basis of their race?" He said yes. The lunch counters desegregated within weeks.

When the original Freedom Riders were beaten so badly in Alabama that many wanted to stop, Nash organized a second wave of riders from Nashville, insisting the rides continue despite the violence. She was 22 years old. She told her recruits they might not come back alive.

Nash also co-designed the Birmingham campaign strategy with James Bevel in 1963, including the controversial decision to involve children as protesters, which produced the images of fire hoses and police dogs that shocked the nation and forced Kennedy to act.

Top: Diane Nash portrait, early 1960s. Bottom: Nash leading a march in Nashville.
The Fight to Vote
1962 – 1965
Fannie Lou Hamer 1917–1977 Voting Rights / MFDP

Fannie Lou Hamer was a Mississippi sharecropper who went to a SNCC voter registration meeting in 1962 and decided to try to register to vote. She had worked the same plantation since she was a child. When her boss found out she had tried to register, he told her to withdraw or leave. She left.

In 1963, while returning from a voter registration workshop, Hamer and other activists were arrested in Winona, Mississippi. She was taken to a cell and beaten so severely by police that she suffered permanent kidney damage. She was 45 years old.

A year later, she was sitting before the Credentials Committee of the Democratic National Convention, representing the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, a group that had formed to challenge the all-white official Mississippi delegation. Her testimony was carried live on national television.

"All of this is on account of we want to register, to become first-class citizens. And if the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America."

— Fannie Lou Hamer, 1964 Democratic National Convention

President Johnson was so alarmed by the attention she was getting that he called an emergency press conference to pull television cameras away from her testimony. He feared she would cost him Southern Democratic votes. The MFDP was not seated. Hamer kept organizing until her death.

Top: Hamer testifying before the Credentials Committee at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, with the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party banner. Bottom: Hamer at the convention in Atlantic City, NJ.

Analysis Questions

Answer in complete sentences. Use specific evidence from the profiles above.

1 The Rosa Parks slide in your notes says she was "carefully chosen" to lead the boycott. Based on what you read here about Parks and Jo Ann Robinson, who actually planned the Montgomery Bus Boycott, and why does that distinction matter?
2 Ella Baker deliberately built SNCC to be independent from MLK and SCLC. What was her argument for doing that, and do you think she was right? Use her quote in your answer.
3 Septima Clark and Fannie Lou Hamer both faced serious personal consequences for their activism, Clark lost her job and pension, Hamer was beaten and lost her home. What does this tell you about the risks ordinary people took in the Civil Rights Movement?
4 Look at what all six women have in common. Then consider: why do you think these women's names are largely absent from standard history textbooks? Give at least two possible reasons and evaluate which you think is most important.
